lesson_title: Steps of the Same Size: Arithmetic Sequences
hook_text: A delivery scooter that adds 7 rand a kilometre — can the fare ever land on exactly 150? One formula knows.
clip_script: A delivery scooter charges 4 rand for the first kilometre and 7 rand for every kilometre after that. One kilometre, 4 rand. Two, 11. Three, 18. You could tick your way to any distance — or think like the rider: begin with 4, add 7 for each kilometre AFTER the first. That is the general term: a plus n minus one, times d. The n minus one matters — the first kilometre is the starting fee, not an add-on. Now the exam question: you carry 88 rand. How far? Seven n minus three equals eighty-eight, so n is thirteen. Exactly thirteen kilometres. But try 150 rand. Seven n minus three equals one fifty puts n at twenty-one comma eight five seven. There is no kilometre twenty-one comma eight five seven. The display steps from 144 straight to 151 — it never shows 150. When n refuses to be whole, the amount was never in the sequence. And that sentence, not a rounded guess, is the answer that earns the mark. Start plus jumps times step, and n must come out whole.
visual_style: A delivery scooter's fare display ticking up in equal jumps along a suburban street, kilometre markers drawn as staircase steps, a banknote hovering between two steps and slipping through the gap at 150.
pacing: Steady ticks through the fares, a hard stop on the 150 question, calm certainty on the close.
